analysis: Examined the two head_text units of fixtures/prompt-contract/v1/production_vectors.json (lines ~34876-36291). They contain public synthetic test vectors for the prompt contract: request_body, provider_body, template_input, plan (prompt_contract_id, block boundaries, chain hashes) and token_ids for the gpt-oss-20b tool-calls, json_object and json_schema cases. The user text is the literal string "Public synthetic cache-parity input" repeated, with no secrets, credentials, keys, attestation material or real consumer data. No executable code, authorization, attestation, encryption or routing logic changes in the supplied units. The patch excerpt for this file (truncated) shows an additional_context {enable_thinking:false} member added to a template_input, changed prompt token counts, and regenerated chain hashes for another vector (a Qwen-style one). Those changes are visible only in the patch hunk, not the head units. Threat relevance is limited to T-041 (prefix-cache and block-boundary keying): the fixtures pin chain_hash/prompt_contract_id values consumed by tests, and are not runtime trust inputs. One unverified contract: the prompt_contract_id in the supplied vectors (a60ed9ae...) is unchanged here, while the patch shows a different ID (8171fec3...) for the altered vector. Whether the consumer and provider implementations that generate and verify these vectors were updated consistently, and whether the new additional_context field is validated on the provider side, is outside the supplied evidence; no source for it was provided. This looks like a test fixture update, with no security regression identified. Integration should confirm the Swift/Go code changes producing these vectors do not weaken cache-key domain separation.
